cells.tense: The practice is running now and it is yours to steer.
cells.ask: Say out loud what this season of practice is for — one sentence, no hedging — and let it set what stays in the routine and what goes.
cells.core: You've got a practice that runs without being forced. Same sit, same stretch, same hour — repeated enough that the body knows it and you're not negotiating with yourself about whether to start. The aloneness is chosen, and strange as that sounds, it's how you stay in touch with people: you come out full instead of running on empty. Refining is steady work here, not a tightness you're managing. That's the thing about endings — some of what you carried was there to get you to this run. Now it's handled by other people and other seasons, and it can go. That's not loss. That's room. Keep the practice light enough to keep going, though. It works because you keep turning up, not because it's impressive — and one honest look at what a session is for tells you which parts to keep and which to drop.
cells.sheetLine: The practice runs without force and you're choosing what it's for.
cells.verb: keeping a small light lit by attention
cells.place: the room where what's finished has to end

cells.tense: You're bracing for how this all ends before the next session has even started.
cells.ask: Pick the one piece of practice you'd keep if everything else had to go, and end the rest of the routine today — only that piece stays.
cells.core: You're refining past the point refining helps. Another pass, another fix, one more week before it's ready — and the practice that used to steady you has turned into a standard you can't put down. The solitude isn't chosen now. It's what protecting the work looks like from the outside, and it's starting to cost you the people who'd make it lighter. Somewhere in there you're keeping ahead of an ending you can't see the shape of, so nothing is allowed to be finished. Finishing is the point of where you're standing. What ends cleanly makes room. What gets held past its time takes up the space anyway. Letting one piece be done isn't quitting the practice. It's how the practice keeps breathing, and it's how you find out which part was actually yours.
cells.sheetLine: Refining has stopped being practice and started being armor.

cells.tense: You stopped in front of this door and you are still standing there.
cells.ask: Do five minutes of the practice once, today or tomorrow, and leave it there even if it went well — the second day is whatever it is.
cells.core: Doing something on your own for its own sake reads as risky before you even begin, so the small daily thing doesn't hold. Not because you don't care — because starting it feels like opening a door you already closed. That's a real caution, not laziness, and arguing with it doesn't help. What you can do is keep a small promise that costs almost nothing, and let the care go both ways in the smallest exchange. Hand something back to someone with the same honesty you'd want from them. It won't feel like discipline. It'll feel like getting the room clear enough to move in — and whether the five minutes turns into six is a different question from whether you showed up at all. Ending what's over doesn't require you to have started anything big.
cells.sheetLine: The starting feels dangerous and small enough is still enough.

cells.tense: You're already doing the work and telling yourself it just happens on its own.
cells.ask: Write down the practice you actually did this week — the unlabeled one — and name it in plain words as something you do.
cells.core: You already do the disciplined thing. The same route on foot, the same pages before anyone's awake, the same attention to detail nobody asked for — you call it habit, or just how you are, or you don't call it anything. So when it's time to end something, you don't notice you're already inside that too: the practices and relationships have quietly started clearing their own space, and you're still describing the clearing as something that happens to you. It isn't. A version of this keeps showing up without asking your permission. It gets easier to steer once you say out loud that it's yours — and once you can hold an unclear map without forcing it to be complete, you can stop bracing for the ending and start walking toward it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already practicing, you just haven't claimed it.
